evidence_quotes.quote: Schemes served between 25 and 7000 households, (median 219). In the wet and dry seasons, users on average spent 30 min collecting 50 L per household per day and 90 min, 80 L, respectively.
Flow rate was measured to represent the ease and availability of water service to users.

Fees were collected at 77 (88 %) water points: 37 collected fees per month and 38 collected fees per jerrican. The average monthly fee was 0.16USD (3 birr) and average fee charge per jerrican was 0.02USD (0.3 birr).
Nearly all committees (89 %) had bylaws that guided the use of the scheme, and 95 % of those reported that the community was aware of the bylaws.
We conducted direct observations of water sources and interviewed water committee members about governance in two regions of Ethiopia.
Values for the summed functionality score ranged from 0 (not functional) to 8 (highly functional). Functionality scores were the primary outcome for our analysis

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community drinking-water service access via 89 rural community-managed water schemes (handpumps, deep wells, and protected springs with and without distribution systems) serving 25 to 7,000 households (median 219) in SNNPR and Oromia, Ethiopia.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study directly examines community water-committee governance, management, accountability, and finance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, while some tested variables reflect operational maintenance capacity or community consultation, the study explicitly measures and models rule-type mechanisms directly governing water service sustainability and availability: tariff and cost-recovery rules (whether a collection fee is charged, monthly tariff amount, per-jerrican tariff amount, and tariff increases over time), formal scheme bylaws guiding use of the water scheme (present in 89% of committees), regular committee elections, record-keeping rules, and periodic external financial audits of committee records by local government officials (present in 65% of schemes). Per the 2026-10-14 results-blindness rule, the statistical significance or non-significance of specific rules (e.g., significant positive associations for higher monthly fees and periodic financial audits; non-significant estimates for bylaws and binary fee charging) does not affect eligibility.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary quantitative empirical cross-sectional study combining direct observations at 89 rural water points with semi-structured interviews of water committee members, analyzed using Mokken scale analysis, univariate logistic regression (n = 82), and univariate linear regression (n = 72).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports two water service availability and reliability/functionality outcomes at the water-scheme level: (1) binary operational status (operational vs. non-operational, where score 0 indicates no water available on the day of visit) and (2) an ordinal/continuous composite functionality score (0-8) incorporating flow rate (time to fill a 20 L jerrican, measuring ease and availability of water service to users), regulated opening/closing hours, drainage, and construction quality.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (community water schemes >= 5 years old in SNNPR and Oromia, Ethiopia; n = 89 surveyed, n = 82 scored), exposures (tariff/cost-recovery rules, formal bylaws, local government financial audits, record keeping, elections, caretaker arrangements, and repair capacity), outcomes (binary operational status and 0-8 functionality score), and study design (cross-sectional observational survey and direct water-point observation) are all clearly specified, with odds ratios, linear regression beta coefficients, and 95% confidence intervals reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional observational study combining direct water-point observations and semi-structured interviews with water committee members, analyzed with Mokken scaling, univariate logistic regression, and univariate linear regression
population_and_sample: 89 purposively sampled rural community-managed drinking-water schemes aged 5 to 44 years (45 handpumps, 21 deep wells, 16 protected springs with distribution, 7 protected springs; serving 25 to 7,000 households, median 219) across 3 districts in SNNPR and 8 districts in Oromia, Ethiopia (n = 82 with complete functionality scores; n = 72 operational schemes in linear regression). Unit of analysis: community water scheme / water point.
exposure: Community water-scheme governance, institutional accountability, and tariff/cost-recovery rules: user fee charging (yes/no), monthly tariff amount (birr), per-jerrican fee amount (birr), fee increases over time, presence and community awareness of formal bylaws guiding scheme use, periodic financial audits of committee records by local government officials, financial record keeping, regular committee elections and meetings, presence and compensation of a scheme caretaker, committee repair capacity, and community consultation.
outcome: Community water-scheme service availability and functionality: (1) binary operational status (operational score >= 1 vs. non-operational score = 0 with no water) among n = 82 schemes, and (2) composite functionality score (0 to 8 scale combining observed water flow rate to fill a 20 L jerrican, regulated opening/closing schedule, drainage, and construction quality) among n = 72 operational schemes.
rationale: This English-language empirical cross-sectional study examines 89 rural community-managed drinking-water schemes in two regions of Ethiopia (SNNPR and Oromia), satisfying all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Alongside maintenance and committee-management indicators, the study explicitly measures and models rule-type governance and cost-recovery mechanisms directly governing community water service availability and functionality—specifically tariff and cost-recovery rules (whether collection fees are charged, monthly fee levels, per-jerrican fee levels, and fee increases over time), formal scheme bylaws guiding use of the water point, regular elections, record keeping, and periodic financial audits by local government officials—against observed water-scheme operational status (presence of water) and a composite 0-8 service functionality score (flow rate, regulated opening/closing hours, drainage, and construction quality), reporting extractable odds ratios and linear regression coefficients.
